text.p: A growing number of companies do not mind if a spouse goes on the road with a business traveller, but fewer than ever are willing to pay for it.
That information comes from a survey of 282 travel managers in the United States by Runzheimer International, a Wisconsin-based consulting firm that polls corporate travel habits.

The latest survey found that slightly more than half of companies polled allow a spouse to go along but do not pay for the spouse's travel. That compared to less than a third of companies with that policy in 1988.

Thirty-nine percent of the firms said they would pay but only provided the traveller was an executive and his or her spouse's presence would somehow benefit the company. But that figure was the lowest level for that type of policy since the surveys began in 1988.
Only 11 percent had a flat no-spouse travel policy and 14 percent allowed for a spouse on long-term assignments.

The survey also found that the trend in corporate America was edging toward companies claiming frequent-flier miles as company property instead of letting the traveller keep them. But nearly four of five companies still do not attempt to recapture the points for their own use.

Eighty-two percent of the companies in the survey said they let the employee keep the mileage points, compared to 88 percent four years ago. Eight percent of those questioned said they had an arrangement calling for the company and the traveller to share the points.

The survey also found that 20 percent of companies allow employees to arrange corporate travel to build up their own frequent-flier accounts while 37 percent have no policy on the subject and the most companies, 43 percent, forbid it.
